name: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
statement: The more precisely you fix a particle's position, the less its momentum can be defined.
statementAccent: the less its momentum can be defined
meaning: There is a fundamental limit to how precisely certain complementary pairs of properties — most famously a particle's position and momentum — can both be defined at once. The product of their uncertainties cannot fall below a fixed minimum, roughly half the reduced Planck constant. A particle prepared with a sharp position has a genuinely undefined momentum, and the reverse.
mechanism: It is rooted in the wave nature of matter. Position and momentum are conjugate variables related by a Fourier transform: a wavefunction sharply localised in position is necessarily spread out in momentum, and vice versa. Formally, the bound follows from the way the two observables fail to commute. Crucially, the rigorous principle concerns the preparation of quantum states, not clumsy measurement — the limit holds even for a particle that has never been touched by any instrument.

examples.text: The canonical pair: the product of the spreads in a particle's position and momentum cannot be smaller than about half the reduced Planck constant, no matter how the state is prepared.

A wave passing a narrow slit has a well-defined position there but spreads out in angle beyond it; narrowing the slit sharpens position and widens the diffraction, trading one uncertainty for the other.
Because a particle cannot have both a definite position and zero momentum, quantum systems retain a minimum energy even at absolute zero, such as the residual energy of a harmonic oscillator.

variants.name: The Robertson-Schrodinger relation
variants.text: The general form bounding the uncertainties of any two observables by their commutator, of which the position-momentum relation is the famous special case.

variants.name: The energy-time relation
variants.text: A related inequality tying the spread in energy to a characteristic time, but with a different logical status, since time is a parameter in quantum mechanics rather than an observable.

whyItMatters: It is a defining feature of quantum mechanics, marking a fundamental break from classical physics: nature itself, not our instruments, sets a limit on how sharply complementary quantities can be defined. It explains the stability and size of atoms, the energy of the quantum vacuum, and the widths of spectral lines.

working.lead: Trade one precision for the other
working.text: when position is pinned down, expect momentum to become correspondingly ill-defined, and the reverse.

working.lead: Read it as a property of nature
working.text: treat the limit as intrinsic to the quantum state, not as a shortcoming of measuring equipment that better tools could beat.
understand the conjugate quantity as genuinely undefined, not merely hidden, unlike ordinary classical ignorance.

limits: The single most important caveat is that the rigorous principle is about intrinsic statistical spread, not measurement disturbance. Heisenberg's original 1927 picture of a microscope knocking the electron — the 'observer effect' — is a distinct idea, and modern work shows measurement error-disturbance relations are separate from the fundamental preparation bound. The energy-time relation has a different status, since time is not an observable in standard quantum mechanics. And the principle is not about experimental clumsiness: no improvement in instruments can beat the limit.
misreadings: It is not the observer effect — it does not merely say that measuring a particle disturbs it; the limit holds for particles never measured, arising from the quantum state itself. And it is fundamental, not instrumental: better technology cannot evade it, and the conjugate quantity is undefined, not just unknown.
origin: Introduced by Werner Heisenberg in a 1927 paper in Zeitschrift fur Physik, where he argued it semi-quantitatively via a microscope thought experiment; Earle Kennard gave the rigorous inequality the same year, and Howard Robertson generalised it in 1929.

sources.text: The Uncertainty Principle, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the history, the Heisenberg/Kennard/Robertson development, and the preparation-versus-disturbance distinction.
Uncertainty principle, Wikipedia. — the inequality forms and the Robertson-Schrodinger generalisation.
